design_detail: Two systematic reviews with country-specific random-effects meta-analyses (Freeman-Tukey double arcsine transformation), combined with modelling: (a) prevalence of any alcohol use during pregnancy among women in the general population (studies published January 1984 to June 2014; 328 studies, 50 countries) and (b) prevalence of fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS) in the general population (November 1973 to June 2015; 62 studies, 19 countries). Drinking prevalence was pooled for the 29 countries with two or more studies and predicted for 158 countries by fractional response regression (GDP per capita, women's alcohol consumption, WHO region); FAS was pooled for 7 countries and, for 180 countries, computed by applying a quotient of 67 women who drank in pregnancy per FAS case (derived from 7 countries) to the drinking prevalence. Monte Carlo confidence intervals; WHO regional and global averages weighted by live births; all estimates labelled 2012. PROSPERO CRD42016033835 and CRD42016033837.
can_establish: Pooled prevalence of reported alcohol use during pregnancy in the general population for the 29 countries with two or more studies, and of FAS for the 7 countries with meta-analysed data, from studies published up to mid-2014 and mid-2015, together with model-based working estimates for all other WHO member states.
cannot_establish: Measured prevalence for most countries (158 of 187 drinking estimates and 180 of 187 FAS estimates are model predictions); the amount, pattern or timing of drinking (not analysed); the risk of FAS for a woman who drinks a given amount (the 1-in-67 figure is a ratio of aggregate prevalences in 7 countries, not a dose-response risk); the prevalence of FASD as a whole (FAS only); trends over time (studies from 1984 to 2014 are pooled into one estimate labelled 2012); or prevalence in special populations (excluded).

sample.recruitment: Alcohol use in pregnancy: 14 databases (Canadian Centre on Substance Abuse Library Collection Database, Campbell Collaboration, CINAHL, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, CSA Sociological Abstracts, Embase, ERIC, Google Scholar, MEDLINE, NIAAA Alcohol and Alcohol Problems Science Database, PsycINFO, Scopus, Social Work Abstracts, Web of Science), January 1, 1984 to June 30, 2014, without language or geographic restriction, plus contents pages of three epidemiology journals and citation screening. FAS: 7 databases (CINAHL, Embase, ERIC, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, Scopus, Web of Science), November 1, 1973 to June 30, 2015, without language or geographic restriction, human studies where the database allowed, plus contents pages of three paediatric epidemiology journals and citation screening (Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: original quantitative research in a peer-reviewed journal or scholarly report reporting the prevalence of alcohol use during pregnancy, or of FAS with a CI, SE, sample size or case count, in the general population of a country. Excluded: samples from special populations (for drinking, for example Indigenous women, adolescents, women of low socioeconomic status, women with HIV or with an alcohol use disorder; for FAS, also Indigenous and correctional populations, children in care and children of women with an alcohol use disorder), pooled estimates from several studies, duplicate publications and, for drinking, studies that excluded abstainers. Where a study gave several drinking estimates, preference went to the estimate after pregnancy recognition, over the whole pregnancy, within 6 weeks post partum, or by a validated method (Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.demographics: Not in the main text: characteristics of the included drinking and FAS studies are in the appendix (pp 4-16 and 28-31), which was not read. Of the 62 FAS studies, 22 used active case ascertainment, 20 passive surveillance, 14 were clinic-based and 6 used mixed methods; 40 used an established diagnostic guideline or stated their case definition (Results, 3rd paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: Restriction to the general population removes groups with much higher prevalence (the Discussion cites 60.5% drinking in pregnancy among Inuit women in northern Quebec and FAS at 92.6 per 10,000 in an Indigenous Australian population). FAS data come from 19 countries in four WHO regions, none in the Eastern Mediterranean or South-East Asia regions, and the authors note that FAS studies were most often regionally confined to areas where high prevalence was expected. Countries with a single study were not meta-analysed: 21 of the 50 countries with drinking data (those with one study, or a meta-analysis giving an interval of 0 to 100%) were assigned a model prediction instead of their observed estimate (editors' arithmetic: 50 minus 29).

exposure.measurement: Alcohol use during pregnancy as measured in each primary study, mostly by self-report questionnaire or interview, in some studies by a validated screening method (the appraisal scored validated method vs questionnaire). No biomarker-based estimate is reported separately in the main text.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Any amount at any time in pregnancy. Quantity, frequency, binge drinking and timing were not analysed because they were not reported or were reported inconsistently (Discussion, 5th paragraph), although the registered protocol named binge drinking (4 or more standard drinks on one occasion) as an outcome. No drink size is defined.

comparison.controls: Not applicable (prevalence review). Denominators: pregnant or recently delivered women in the general population for drinking; general-population samples of children of various ages, including newborns in clinic-based studies, for FAS.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to prevalence. The FAS quotient assumes the same ratio of FAS cases to women who drank in pregnancy in every country; drinking pattern, nutrition, smoking, stress, genetic background and diagnostic practice, which the paper names as modifiers of fetal vulnerability, are not modelled.

outcomes.instruments: Prevalence of any alcohol use during pregnancy (%) and of FAS (per 10,000 people), with FAS diagnosed by varied systems or case definitions. The primary FAS analysis used studies with active case ascertainment or clinic-based methods and a specified guideline or case definition; a secondary analysis added passive-surveillance studies and studies without a stated definition (Methods › Meta-analyses, 5th paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: Drinking studies were appraised in duplicate on four criteria based on Wong et al. (2008): probability vs non-probability sampling, a sample of at least 300, validated method vs questionnaire, and response or participation of at least 70%. FAS studies were appraised in duplicate on the ten criteria of Munn et al. (2014). The appraisal results are in the appendix (pp 21-26 and 37-38), not read (Methods › Meta-analyses, 1st and 4th paragraphs).
outcomes.operationalization: FAS prevalence per 10,000 people in the general population; the annual number of births with FAS applies the global prevalence to 81,536,534 live births. All estimates are labelled 2012 although the pooled studies span 1984 to 2014 (drinking) and 1973 to 2015 (FAS).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Two investigators did each selection step and the quality appraisal independently; one extracted the data and a second cross-checked them independently against the original studies, with discrepancies settled by team discussion; non-English studies were translated by fluent colleagues or with Google Translate checked by a native speaker (Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria, 3rd paragraph; Methods › Meta-analyses, 1st paragraph).

analysis.effect_sizes: Any alcohol use during pregnancy in 2012, weighted by live births (Table): global 9.8% (95% CI 8.9-11.1); European region 25.2% (21.6-29.6); Americas 11.2% (9.4-12.6); African region 10.0% (8.5-11.8); Western Pacific 8.6% (4.5-11.6); South-East Asia 1.8% (0.9-5.1); Eastern Mediterranean 0.2% (0.1-0.9). Highest countries: Ireland 60.4% (42.8-76.8), Belarus 46.6% (42.4-50.7; predicted), Denmark 45.8% (30.9-61.2), UK 41.3% (lower limit 32.9; upper limit misprinted), Russia 36.5% (18.7-56.4); lowest, 0% by prediction: Oman, United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Kuwait. FAS per 10,000 people (Table): global 14.6 (9.4-23.3); European region 37.4 (24.7-54.2); Americas 16.6 (11.0-24.0); African region 14.8 (8.9-21.5); Western Pacific 12.7 (7.7-19.4); South-East Asia 2.7 (1.3-8.1); Eastern Mediterranean 0.2 (0.2-0.9). Highest countries: South Africa 585.3 (430.7-761.7), Croatia 115.2 (34.8-236.0), Ireland 89.7 (50.4-142.8; predicted), Italy 82.1 (42.1-134.6), Belarus 69.1 (42.1-103.5; predicted). Quotient: one FAS case per 67 women who drank during pregnancy, from Australia, Canada, Croatia, France, Italy, South Korea and the USA, giving about 119,000 children with FAS born each year. Heterogeneity statistics and publication-bias tests are reported only in the appendix (pp 20 and 35); no prediction intervals.
analysis.covariates: Prediction of drinking prevalence for countries with one or no study: fractional response regression (generalised linear model, binomial family, logit link) on GDP per capita at purchasing power parity (World Bank), women's mean total alcohol consumption (WHO Global Information System on Alcohol and Health) and WHO region, with the European region split into EU and non-EU states and the Americas into Canada and the USA vs the rest; other candidate variables in the appendix (Methods › Meta-analyses, 2nd paragraph).
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42016033835 (alcohol use in pregnancy) and CRD42016033837 (FAS and FASD), both registered on 31 January 2016 (PROSPERO records read), after the searches had closed in June 2014 and June 2015; at registration the alcohol-use record marks searching, screening and data extraction as completed. Deviations not explained in the paper: the alcohol-use protocol planned binge-drinking prevalence, estimates for Aboriginal or Indigenous and low-socioeconomic-status populations and by method of ascertainment (self-report, meconium, other biomarkers), and exact confidence intervals for countries with a single study; the paper reports any use only, excludes special populations, and replaces single-study countries with predictions (fractional response regression for drinking, the quotient for FAS), methods neither record describes. The FAS record also planned FASD estimates, reported separately in Lange et al. (2017).
analysis.selective_reporting: Binge drinking, planned in the protocol, is not reported. Country estimates, heterogeneity and publication-bias results and appraisal results are confined to the appendix and the maps. The main text does not say which seven countries had meta-analysed FAS estimates.
analysis.power: Not applicable as such. The FAS quotient rests on seven countries, and FAS meta-analyses exist for seven countries; every FAS figure outside those countries inherits the quotient's uncertainty.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Pooling reported drinking in pregnancy from 328 general-population studies and modelling the remaining countries, about 1 in 10 pregnant women worldwide (9.8%) and about 1 in 4 in the WHO European region (25.2%) drank some alcohol during pregnancy, with estimates near zero in the Eastern Mediterranean region. FAS prevalence was estimated at 14.6 per 10,000 globally and 37.4 in the European region. Because FAS was measured in 19 countries and meta-analysed in 7, the regional and global FAS figures are in effect the drinking prevalence divided by 67 (editors' arithmetic: 9.8% / 67 = 14.6 per 10,000; 25.2% / 67 = 37.6; 10.0% / 67 = 14.9).
interpretation_gap.claimed: (1) The Summary says "one in every 67 women who consumed alcohol during pregnancy would deliver" a child with FAS, which reads as an individual risk; it is a ratio of two aggregate prevalences in seven countries, applied unchanged to 180 others, and the Discussion's own explanation of South Africa's high FAS prevalence (a binge pattern among women who drink) shows the ratio varies with drinking pattern. (2) The 119,000 births a year apply a prevalence measured in general-population samples of children, stated per 10,000 people, to live births; the paper calls the same figure per 10,000 people in the Summary, Results and Discussion and per 10,000 livebirths in the Research in context panel. (3) Estimates labelled 2012 pool studies from 1984 to 2014 without allowing for time. (4) The Interpretation and Discussion call FAS a relatively prevalent birth defect and speculate that its prevalence could increase, from mostly modelled figures, while the authors acknowledge that the FAS studies were done where high prevalence was expected. (5) The Discussion's comparison for the USA with anencephaly, spina bifida, trisomy 18 and trisomy 21 is made without the US estimate in the main text. Against this, the limitations paragraph is candid about self-report, unvalidated tools, diagnostic inconsistency and prediction error.

timeline.event: Jones and Smith (1973), Recognition of the fetal alcohol syndrome in early infancy (Lancet 302:999-1001), cited as the first description of FAS and the start date of the FAS search; this is not the Jones et al. 1973 paper held as jones_1973.
Abel (1995): FAS in 4.3% of children born to pregnant women who drank heavily (about 1 in 23), cited in the Discussion as consistent with the quotient of 1 in 67 for any drinking.

Correction (Lancet Glob Health 2017; 5: e276; doi 10.1016/S2214-109X(17)30032-3; online 25 January 2017): figures 2 and 4 had been published in the wrong order, and values for Australia and China (drinking map) and for Australia, Jamaica, Kazakhstan, Lesotho, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan (FAS map) were corrected to match appendix tables A2 and A7. The notice lists no change to the text or the Table.

Tsang and Elliott, linked Comment (Lancet Glob Health 2017; 5: e232-e233; doi 10.1016/S2214-109X(17)30008-6): supportive; notes that few included studies were truly population-based or national, that only 16.5% used a validated method to identify the level of risk from prenatal alcohol exposure (their figure; not in this paper's main text), that patterns of exposure were not analysed and diagnostic criteria vary, and that excluding special populations may make the estimates conservative.

Lange et al. (2017), companion FASD meta-analysis by the same team from the same FAS search, using these drinking estimates: FASD 7.7 per 1000 children and youth, one FASD case per 13 women who drank (card sc_lange_2017).

In their reply to a JAMA Pediatrics letter by Pichini, Pacifici and Busardò about the Italian FASD estimate, Lange, Rehm and Popova state that the same writers had raised a similar concern about this paper's FAS estimates in The Lancet Global Health; that correspondence was not located or read.

replication.where_it_stands: The standard source for the figures that about 10% of pregnant women worldwide drink and that FAS affects about 15 per 10,000. Both are dominated by modelling: drinking prevalence is pooled from observations for 29 countries and predicted for 158, and FAS is pooled for 7 countries and computed for the other 180 as the drinking prevalence divided by 67. Claims should separate measured from modelled estimates, describe the 1-in-67 figure as an aggregate ratio from seven countries rather than a woman's risk, and keep FAS distinct from FASD. The FASD companion paper (Lange et al., 2017) inherits these drinking estimates.

funding.funder: Centre for Addiction and Mental Health; no external funding was sought (Summary › Funding). The funder had no role in study design, data collection, analysis, interpretation or writing (Methods › Role of the funding source).
funding.declared_conflicts: None: the authors declare no competing interests (Declaration of interests).
funding.affiliations_note: All five authors are at the Institute for Mental Health Policy Research, Centre for Addiction and Mental Health, Toronto, with University of Toronto, Technische Universität Dresden and University of New South Wales affiliations. The introduction draws on the team's own earlier FASD comorbidity and cost studies, and the same team wrote the companion FASD meta-analysis (Lange et al., 2017). No industry funding or ties are declared.

what_would_settle_it: Nationally representative surveys of pregnant women with validated quantity, frequency and binge measures (with biomarkers in a subsample) in the countries now covered only by prediction, and active-case-ascertainment FAS and FASD studies using one diagnostic system in randomly chosen rather than high-prevalence communities, from which a pattern-specific ratio of FAS cases to exposed pregnancies could be estimated.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (general population of each country; pregnant women for drinking), condition (any alcohol use in pregnancy; FAS), outcome (prevalence) and eligible studies are specified for both reviews.

Both PROSPERO records were registered on 31 January 2016, after the searches closed (June 2014 and June 2015), and the alcohol-use record shows searching, screening and extraction already completed; the paper does not state that methods were set beforehand and does not explain its departures from the records (binge drinking and special populations dropped; single-study countries predicted rather than reported with exact intervals).
Any original quantitative study reporting general-population prevalence, the designs a prevalence question calls for; studies excluding abstainers were excluded with an evident reason.

14 and 7 databases with search terms given, no language restriction, journal hand-searching, citation screening, Google Scholar and scholarly reports admitted; but no contact with experts is reported and the searches closed about 31 months (drinking) and 19 months (FAS) before online publication in January 2017.
Two investigators did each selection step independently, with disagreements settled by team discussion.
One investigator extracted and a second independently cross-checked against the original studies, discrepancies settled by discussion, which meets the item's consensus criterion.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The flow charts (Figures 1 and 3, images) summarize exclusions; no list of excluded full-text studies with reasons appears in the article, and none of the appendix pages cited in the text is described as one (appendix not read).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Provisional: study characteristics are only in the appendix (pp 4-16 and 28-31), which was not read; the main text gives counts by country and FAS ascertainment method only.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Prevalence-appropriate tools applied in duplicate (four criteria based on Wong et al. for drinking studies, ten from Munn et al. for FAS studies), but the drinking checklist does not address under-reporting, the timing of the question in pregnancy or the definition of use, and the results are only in the appendix.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported in the main text.

Within-country random-effects pooling of double-arcsine-transformed proportions is a standard technique, but the paper gives no justification for pooling studies spanning 30 years into one estimate labelled 2012, or for pooling different definitions and timings of drinking; heterogeneity statistics are not reported in the article and no prediction intervals are given; observed single-study data are replaced by model predictions; and the FAS quotient assumes one ratio for all countries. Judged on the item's requirement that combining the data be justified; a close call for the within-country pooling alone.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No analysis of the drinking estimates by study quality; for FAS, the secondary analysis adding passive surveillance and undefined cases is a related sensitivity analysis (lower estimates for Australia, France, Italy and the USA), but the drinking estimates on which all modelled FAS figures rest were not examined.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The limitations paragraph discusses non-representative sampling, unvalidated tools, self-report under-reporting, diagnostic inconsistency, prediction error and FAS studies done where high prevalence was expected.
Heterogeneity tests are reported only in the appendix (pp 20 and 35); the article neither reports nor discusses heterogeneity.

Funnel plots, a rank correlation test and a weighted regression test were run, with results only in the appendix; the article does not discuss the likelihood or likely impact of publication or small-study bias.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Institutional funding stated, no external funding sought, no competing interests declared.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional, because item 8 could be judged only from the unread appendix; the rating would not change. Four critical items are not met (2, protocol registered after the searches; 7, no list of excluded studies; 11, combining unjustified and heterogeneity unreported; 15, publication bias not discussed), and two are partly met (4 and 9), which by the AMSTAR 2 rule gives critically low confidence in the pooled and modelled figures. This is a judgment on how far the numbers can be taken as unbiased summaries, not on the effort: searches were broad and language-unrestricted, selection and appraisal were duplicated, and the limitations are stated plainly. The practical point for claims is that most country, regional and global figures are model outputs, and the FAS figures outside seven countries are a fixed fraction of the drinking estimates.

key_findings.finding: Alcohol use in pregnancy: of 23,470 records, 328 studies were retained, with general-population data from 50 countries in all six WHO regions. FAS: of 11,110 records, 62 studies were retained, with data from 19 countries in four WHO regions (African, Americas, European, Western Pacific).

Drinking prevalence was estimated by random-effects meta-analysis for 29 countries and by fractional response regression for 158 countries with one or no study; FAS prevalence by meta-analysis for 7 countries and, for 180 countries, by applying the quotient of women who drank per FAS case to the country's drinking prevalence.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd and 4th paragraphs; Methods › Meta-analyses, 2nd and 6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Prevalence of any alcohol use during pregnancy in the general population in 2012, weighted by live births: global 9.8% (95% CI 8.9-11.1); European region 25.2% (21.6-29.6), highest; Americas 11.2% (9.4-12.6); African region 10.0% (8.5-11.8); Western Pacific 8.6% (4.5-11.6); South-East Asia 1.8% (0.9-5.1); Eastern Mediterranean 0.2% (0.1-0.9), lowest.

Country extremes for drinking in pregnancy: Ireland 60.4% (42.8-76.8), Belarus 46.6% (42.4-50.7; predicted), Denmark 45.8% (30.9-61.2), UK 41.3% (from 32.9; upper limit misprinted), Russia 36.5% (18.7-56.4); 0% (predicted) in Oman, United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Kuwait.

FAS prevalence in the general population per 10,000 people: global 14.6 (95% CI 9.4-23.3); European region 37.4 (24.7-54.2); Americas 16.6 (11.0-24.0); African region 14.8 (8.9-21.5); Western Pacific 12.7 (7.7-19.4); South-East Asia 2.7 (1.3-8.1); Eastern Mediterranean 0.2 (0.2-0.9).

Highest country FAS estimates per 10,000: South Africa 585.3 (430.7-761.7), Croatia 115.2 (34.8-236.0), Ireland 89.7 (50.4-142.8; predicted), Italy 82.1 (42.1-134.6), Belarus 69.1 (42.1-103.5; predicted); below 0.05 (predicted) in Oman, United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Kuwait.

From the seven countries with both indicators (Australia, Canada, Croatia, France, Italy, South Korea, USA), one in every 67 women who drank during pregnancy delivered a child with FAS; applied to 81,536,534 live births, about 119,000 children with FAS are born each year.
key_findings.note: An aggregate ratio of two prevalences, not an individual risk; editors' arithmetic: 14.6 per 10,000 times 81,536,534 is about 119,000.

key_findings.finding: Editors' arithmetic from the Table: the regional and global FAS estimates equal, within rounding, the regional drinking prevalence divided by 67: global 9.8% / 67 = 14.6 per 10,000 (printed 14.6); European 25.2% / 67 = 37.6 (37.4); African 10.0% / 67 = 14.9 (14.8); Americas 11.2% / 67 = 16.7 (16.6); Western Pacific 8.6% / 67 = 12.8 (12.7); South-East Asia 1.8% / 67 = 2.7 (2.7).
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic; it shows the FAS figures outside the seven meta-analysed countries carry no independent FAS information.

key_findings.finding: The secondary FAS analysis, which added passive-surveillance studies and studies without a stated diagnostic definition, gave lower point estimates for Australia, France, Italy and the USA; values are in the appendix (p 36).

The Discussion compares the quotient with Abel's estimate that 4.3% of children born to pregnant women who drink heavily (an average of two or more drinks a day, or five to six per occasion) have FAS, about 1 in 23, three times the general-population quotient; and cites a ratio of FAS to FASD of about 1 to 9 or 10, calling FAS the tip of the iceberg.

Limitations stated by the authors: some included drinking studies used non-representative samples or unvalidated tools; self-reported drinking may be under-reported, so drinking and FAS prevalence may be underestimated; drinking patterns not analysed; FAS diagnostic guidelines inconsistent or unspecified; predictions carry measurement error and omit variables such as alcohol policies; FAS studies were mostly regionally confined to areas of expected high prevalence; WHO member states only.

Both PROSPERO records (CRD42016033835 for drinking in pregnancy, CRD42016033837 for FAS and FASD) were registered on 31 January 2016; the drinking record, with a review start date of 1 January 2013, marks searching, screening and data extraction as already completed and plans binge-drinking prevalence, Indigenous and low-socioeconomic-status subgroups and exact intervals for single-study countries.
key_findings.locator: PROSPERO CRD42016033835 and CRD42016033837: Timeline of the review; Stage of the review; Planned data synthesis; Analysis of subgroups

key_findings.finding: The version read is the corrected online version of 25 January 2017. The correction (doi 10.1016/S2214-109X(17)30032-3) concerns only figures 2 and 4: the maps had been printed in the wrong order, and values for Australia and China (drinking map) and Australia, Jamaica, Kazakhstan, Lesotho, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan (FAS map) were corrected to match appendix tables A2 and A7.
key_findings.locator: Correction to Lancet Glob Health 2017; 5: e290-99 (Lancet Glob Health 2017; 5: e276); article page, note after the Discussion
key_findings.note: No number on this card comes from the maps, so none is affected by the correction.

reporting_issues.issue: The UK's drinking prevalence is printed as 41.3% with an interval of 32.9 to 49.%, the upper limit incomplete.
reporting_issues.consequence: The UK interval cannot be quoted from the main text; the appendix (not read) would be needed.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion gives FAS in children in a Brazilian orphanage (Strömland et al.) as 3191 per 10,000, more than 14 times the general population; that multiple implies a Brazilian general-population FAS prevalence of about 228 per 10,000 (editors' arithmetic), far above the Americas average of 16.6. The companion paper by the same team (Lange et al., 2017, Figure 2 legend) gives FASD in the same orphanage as 170.2 per 1000 (1702 per 10,000), lower than the FAS figure here although FAS is a subset of FASD.
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one of the two figures, and the stated multiple, is wrong; neither should be cited without checking the primary study. One reading that fits both the stated multiple and the FASD figure is a decimal misprint, 319.1 per 10,000 (31.9 per 1,000) for 3191 (second reader's suggestion; not checked against the primary study).

reporting_issues.issue: FAS prevalence is described as per 10,000 people in the Summary, Results and Discussion, and as per 10,000 livebirths in the Research in context panel; the 119,000 annual births apply the former to live births.
reporting_issues.consequence: Prevalence measured in general-population samples of children of various ages is treated as birth prevalence; the annual-births figure should be cited as a model estimate under that assumption.

reporting_issues.issue: The main text does not name the seven countries with meta-analysed FAS estimates. South Africa's estimate (585.3 per 10,000, the highest) is not marked as predicted, so it presumably comes from a meta-analysis, yet South Africa is not among the seven countries named for the quotient (Australia, Canada, Croatia, France, Italy, South Korea, USA); how the two sets of seven relate, and why South Africa's data did not enter the quotient, is not explained.
reporting_issues.consequence: The derivation of the 1-in-67 quotient, which drives 180 of the 187 FAS estimates, cannot be reconstructed from the article.

reporting_issues.issue: The registered protocols planned binge-drinking prevalence, special-population and ascertainment-method subgroups and exact intervals for single-study countries; the paper drops these and introduces prediction models not in the protocols, without comment.
reporting_issues.consequence: Undeclared departures from the protocol; the reasons can only be inferred (the limitations say patterns were inconsistently reported).

reporting_issues.issue: The correction notice cites the original as Lancet Glob Health 2016, published online 12 January, while the article was published online in January 2017.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; the correction's own DOI and pages identify it.
